name: Theobromine
lead: Theobromine is the main alkaloid of the cacao plant (Theobroma cacao) and a dimethylxanthine closely related to caffeine and theophylline. It occurs in cocoa and chocolate, with smaller amounts in tea, yerba mate, kola nut and guarana [1][2]. Reference works describe it as a mild diuretic, heart stimulant and bronchodilator with much weaker central nervous system stimulation than caffeine [1].

In appearance-oriented discussion it is grouped with de-puffing and water-balance compounds because of its diuretic classification. No published study has tested whether theobromine reduces facial puffiness or otherwise changes appearance; the human trials that exist examined mood, cognition, blood pressure, lipids, cough and dental outcomes [3][4].

Because the amount in dietary chocolate is small and the compound is sold as a food ingredient and supplement in many places, it is not a prescription product in most jurisdictions; in South Korea it has been sold as a prescription cough ingredient [1].

paras: Theobromine is a flat, slightly water-soluble purine derivative that differs from caffeine by lacking one methyl group. The name derives from the Greek words for god and food and does not refer to bromine [1]. It is the principal alkaloid in cacao, at roughly 1.5 to 3 percent of the dry bean, with dark chocolate generally containing more than milk chocolate and cocoa powder the most concentrated common food source [1][2]. Commercially it is extracted from cocoa husks left over from chocolate production [2].

Theobromine blocks adenosine receptors and is a weaker phosphodiesterase inhibitor than other methylxanthines [1]. It is more lipid-soluble than caffeine and reaches peak blood levels more slowly, about two to three hours after ingestion, and is metabolised in the liver by CYP1A2 and CYP2E1 enzymes [1][5]. Its elimination half-life is reported as about 6 to 9 hours [1][2]. It is classed among diuretics in the ATC system [1].

Intakes of roughly 0.8 to 1.5 grams per day have been reported to cause sweating, trembling and severe headache [1]. Theobromine is the main reason chocolate is toxic to dogs and cats, which clear it slowly [1][2].

Registered human studies of theobromine have examined acute physiological effects of different serving regimens [3], mood, cognition and blood pressure compared with caffeine [4], blood lipid parameters in 152 healthy subjects [6], vascular function and intestinal apoA-I production [7], and an antitussive capsule in 332 people with acute bronchitis [8]. Others have looked at theobromine toothpaste and dentin hypersensitivity [9][10]. Results are mixed and often confounded when studied as part of cocoa, where flavanols also contribute [2]. No study found has examined theobromine for facial puffiness, water retention or other appearance outcomes.

timeline.event: Theobromine isolated from cacao beans by A. Woskresensky [1].
Emil Fischer reports synthesis from xanthine [1].

card.summary: Cocoa's main xanthine, a mild diuretic with no published evidence for de-puffing.
card.note: Diuretic classification is not backed by appearance studies.

quick.overview:
Theobromine is the main stimulant-like compound in cocoa. It is chemically close to caffeine but acts more weakly on the nervous system.

It is grouped with depuffing compounds because reference works call it a mild diuretic. No study has tested it for facial puffiness or other appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: It blocks adenosine receptors and weakly inhibits phosphodiesterases, with effects on blood vessels, heart and kidneys described in reference works. It is metabolised by liver CYP1A2 and CYP2E1 with a half-life of about 6 to 9 hours.
quick.risks: Reported effects at high intakes include sweating, tremor and headache. It is notably toxic to dogs and cats. Regulatory status is as a food ingredient in most places.
